parts.problem_md:
In recent years, astronomers have discovered sources of fast radio bursts (FRBs) in other galaxies. Studies suggest that these sources may be a type of standard candle.

An FRB source emits intense bursts of radio waves, each burst lasting for a fraction of a second. The closest FRB source is in a massive spiral galaxy 4.60 × 10<sup>24 </sup>m from the Earth. A detector of area 1.00 × 10<sup>−4 </sup>m<sup>2</sup> on the surface of the Earth received bursts of radio waves. In one burst, 9.40 × 10<sup>−23</sup> J of energy was received in a time of 1.15 ms.

(i) Show that the luminosity of the source is about 2 × 10<sup>35 </sup>W.

[4]

(ii) When FRB sources were first discovered, some observers suggested that the bursts might be extraterrestrial communications.

Suggest why this is unlikely.

luminosity of the Sun = 3.8 × 10<sup>26 </sup>W

[2]
parts.solution_md:
(i) Show that the luminosity of the source is about 2 × 10<sup>35 </sup>W:

List the known quantities:

- Distance from Earth, $d$ = 4.60 × 10<sup>24 </sup>m
- Area of detector, $A$ = 1.00 × 10<sup>−4 </sup>m<sup>2</sup>
- Energy of burst, $E$ = 9.40 × 10<sup>−23</sup> J
- Time of burst, $t$ = 1.15 ms = 1.15 × 10<sup>-3 </sup>s

Determine the power of the burst of radio waves:

- Power:  $P=\frac{E}{t}=\frac{9.40\times10^{-23}}{1.15\times10^{-3}}=8.17\times10^{-20}W$ **[1 mark]**

Determine the intensity of the burst:

- Intensity:  $F=\frac{P}{A}=\frac{8.17\times10^{-20}}{1.00\times10^{-4}}=8.17\times10^{-16}Wm^{-2}$ **[1 mark]**

Use the inverse square law of flux equation to find luminosity:

- Inverse square law of flux:  $F=\frac{L}{4πd^{2}}$
- $L = 4 \mathrm{\pi } d^{2} F = 4 \mathrm{\pi } \times ( 4.60 \times 10^{24 )^{2} \times ( 8.17 \times 10^{-16} } )$ **[1 mark]**
- $L=2.17\times10^{35}=2.2\times10^{35}W$ **[1 mark]**

(ii) It is unlikely that FRB sources are extraterrestrial communications because:

- The luminosity of the FRB source is much larger than the luminosity of the Sun; **[1 mark]**
- A power output this large is unlikely to be artificially produced; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 6 marks]**

> *The marks for part (ii) can only be gained if the answer for part (i) is significantly larger than the value given for the Sun's luminosity*

parts.problem_md:
It has been suggested that FRBs are produced by a type of star known as a magnetar.

Magnetars are extremely dense, hot remnants of stars which produce intensely powerful magnetic fields. These magnetic fields power the emission of high-energy radiation, particularly X-rays and gamma rays.

Fig. 1.1 shows how the radiated intensity from a magnetar varies with photon energy.

![25-1-1b-h-25-1-h-magnetar-wien-curve-photon-energy-cie-ial-sq](assets/001-25-1-1b-h-25-1-h-magnetar-wien-curve-photon-ener.png)

**Fig. 1.1**

Using Fig. 1.1, determine the surface temperature of the magnetar.

Wien's displacement constant = 2.898 × 10<sup>−3</sup> m K
parts.solution_md:
Determine the surface temperature of the magnetar:

List the known quantities:

- Wien's displacement constant = 2.898 × 10<sup>−3</sup> m K
- Planck's constant, *h* = 6.63 × 10<sup>−34</sup> J s
- Speed of light, *c* = 3.0 × 10<sup>8</sup> m s<sup>−1</sup>
- 1 eV = 1.6 × 10<sup>−19</sup> J

Use the graph to obtain a value for the maximum energy:

![25-1-1b-h-25-1-h-magnetar-wien-c-ma](assets/002-25-1-1b-h-25-1-h-magnetar-wien-c-ma.png)

- (From the graph) maximum energy, $E_{max}$ = 8 × 10<sup>1</sup> = 80 keV  [1 mark] *Acceptable range for maximum energy = 75 to 80 keV*

Convert the maximum energy into the maximum wavelength:

- Photon energy:  $E=\frac{hc}{λ}\Rightarrowλ_{max}=\frac{hc}{E_{max}}$
- $\lambda_{m a x} = \frac{( 6.63 \times 10^{- 34} ) ( 3.0 \times 10^{8 )}{( 80 \times 10^{3} ) ( 1.6 \times 10^{-19} } )}$
- $λ_{max}$ = 1.554 × 10<sup>−11</sup> m [1 mark] *Acceptable range for max. wavelength = (1.55 to 1.66) × 10*<sup>*−11*</sup>* m*

Use Wien's Law to calculate the temperature of the magnetar:

- Wien's law:  $T\propto\frac{1}{λ_{max}}\Rightarrowλ_{max}T=2.898\times10^{-3}mK$
- $T=\frac{2.898\times10^{-3}}{λ_{max}}=\frac{2.898\times10^{-3}}{1.554\times10^{-11}}$ [1 mark]
- $T$ = 1.865 × 10<sup>8</sup> = 1.9 × 10<sup>8</sup> K [1 mark] *Acceptable range for surface temperature = (1.7 to 1.9) × 10*<sup>*8*</sup>* K*

**[Total: 4 marks]**

(b) Magnetars are extremely dense, hot remnants of stars. Determine the surface temperature of the magnetar: T = 1.865 × 10^8 K

parts.solution_md:
Determine the diameter of the magnetar and compare it to the size of a city:

List the known quantities:

- Luminosity of FRB/magnetar, $L$ = 2.17 × 10<sup>35</sup> W (from **(a)**)
- Surface temperature of the magnetar, $T$ = 1.865 × 10<sup>8</sup> K (from **(b)**)
- Stefan-Boltzmann constant, $σ$ = 5.67 × 10<sup>–8</sup> W m<sup>–2</sup> K<sup>–4</sup>

Use the Stefan-Boltzmann Law to calculate the radius of the magnetar:

- Stefan-Boltzmann Law:  $L=4πR^{2}σT^{4}\RightarrowR=\sqrt{\frac{L}{4πσT^{4}}}$
- Radius:  $R = \sqrt{ \frac{2.17 \times 10^{35}{4 \mathrm{\pi } \times ( 5.67 \times 10^{-8} } ) \times ( 1.865 \times 10^{8} )^{4} } }$ **[1 mark]**
- Radius:  $R=15866=15.9\mathrm{km}$ **[1 mark]**

Estimate the size of a city and compare it to the diameter of the magnetar:

- Diameter of the magnetar = 2 × 15.9 = 31.8 km
- A reasonable estimate for the size of a large city is 10<sup>1</sup> to 10<sup>2</sup> km; **[1 mark]**
- Hence the statement from the literature is correct; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 4 marks]**

parts.problem_md:
In 2017, an ultra-cool star in our galaxy Trappist-1 was discovered with at least five of its own orbiting planets.

Astronomers have studied it extensively to determine if there is a possibility of finding life on some of the planets orbiting Trappist-1.

Table 1.1 below shows some data.

**Table 1.1 **

|   | **Trappist-1** | **Sun** |
|---|---|---|
| **Luminosity *****L / L***<sub>**☉**</sub> | 5.26 × 10<sup>−4</sup> | 1 |
| **Surface temperature *****T / T***<sub>**☉**</sub> | 0.4 | 1 |
| **Radius of star / *****R***<sub>**☉**</sub> | *R* | 1 |
| **Distance between Earth and Sun / m** | − | 1.5 × 10<sup>11</sup> |
| **Distance between planets and Trappist-1 / m** | 1.6 × 10<sup>9</sup> to 9.0 × 10<sup>9</sup> | − |

The temperature *T,* in K, of a planet, its distance *d* from the star and the luminosity *L* of the star are related by the expression

$\frac{T^{4}d^{2}}{L}=419\times10^{3}$

(i) Show that the radius *R* of Trappist-1 is smaller than the radius of the Sun.

[2]

(ii) The average temperature of the Earth is about 290 K.

Using data from Table 1.1, comment on the possibility of life existing on some of the planets orbiting Trappist-1.

[4]
parts.solution_md:
(i) Show that the radius *R* of T-1 is smaller than the radius of the Sun

List the known quantities:

- Luminosity of T-1, *L* = (5.26 × 10<sup>−4</sup>)*L*<sub>☉</sub>
- Surface temperature of T-1, *T* = 0.4*T*<sub>☉</sub>
- Radius of T-1 = *R*

Use the Stefan-Boltzmann law to determine the radius of T-1:

- Stefan-Boltzmann law:  $L=4πr^{2}σT^{4}\RightarrowR=\sqrt{\frac{L}{4πσT^{4}}}$
- Radius of the Sun:  `R _ ☉ = sqrt( (L _ ☉)/(4 pi sigma ( T _ ☉ ) ^ 4) )`
- Radius of T-1:  `R = sqrt( (( 5.26 x 10 ^ - 4 ) L _ ☉)/(4 pi sigma ( 0.4 T _ ☉ ) ^ 4) )`
- Radius of T-1:  `R = sqrt( (5.26 x 10 ^ - 4 )/(0.4 ^ 4) ) x R _ ☉ = 0.14 R _ ☉` **[1 mark]**

Conclusion:

- 0.14 < 1, therefore, the radius of T-1 is smaller than the radius of the Sun; **[1 mark]**

(ii) Consider whether life may be possible on some of the planets orbiting Trappist-1:

List the known quantities:

- Earth-Sun distance = 1.5 × 10<sup>11</sup> m
- Minimum T1-planet distance = 1.6 × 10<sup>9</sup> m
- Maximum T1-planet distance = 9.0 × 10<sup>9</sup> m
- Temperature of Earth = 290 K

Determine the luminosity of T-1:

- (From question):  $\frac{T^{4}d^{2}}{L}=419\times10^{3}\RightarrowL=\frac{T^{4}d^{2}}{419\times10^{3}}$
- Luminosity of the Sun:  `L _ ☉ = (290 ^ 4 x ( 1.5 x 10 ^ 11 ) ^2)/(419 x 10 ^3) = 3.8 x 10 ^ 26 W`
- Luminosity of T-1:  *L* = (5.26 × 10<sup>−4</sup>) × (3.8 × 10<sup>26</sup>) = 2.0 × 10<sup>23</sup> W **[1 mark]**

Determine the range of temperatures of planets around T-1:

- $\frac{T^{4} d^{2}}{L} = 419 \times 10^{3} \Leftrightarrow T = \sqrt[4]{ \frac{L \times ( 419 \times 10^{3} )}{d^{2}} }$
- Inner-most planet temperature:  $T_{m i n} = \sqrt[4]{ \frac{( 419 \times 10^{3} ) \times ( 2.0 \times 10^{23} )}{( 9.0 \times 10^{9} )^{2}} } = 179 \mathrm{K}$
- Outer-most planet temperature:  $T_{m a x} = \sqrt[4]{ \frac{( 419 \times 10^{3} ) \times ( 2.0 \times 10^{23} )}{( 1.6 \times 10^{9} )^{2}} } = 425 \mathrm{K}$
- $T_{min}=180K$  **AND ** $T_{max}=430K$ **[1 mark]**

Write a conclusion:

- With temperatures ranging from 179 to 425 K it is very <u>likely</u> that life could exist on a planet around Trappist-1; **[1 mark]**

**Final answer:** **And max ****one**** from:**

- Trappist-1 is smaller / cooler than the Sun; **[1 mark]**
- The planets orbit closer to Trappist-1; **[1 mark]**
- It is possible for the temperature on the planets to be similar to Earth; **[1 mark]**
- For life to exist, temperature is not the only factor; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 6 marks]**

parts.problem_md: State Wien’s displacement law.
parts.solution_md:
Wien’s displacement law states:

- The wavelength of maximum intensity (emitted by a star) is inversely proportional to its (thermodynamic) temperature **OR**
- $λ_{max}\propto\frac{1}{T}$, where $λ_{max}$ = wavelength of maximum intensity and $T$ = (thermodynamic) temperature; **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 1 mark]**

> *Make sure not just to state the equation, but **explain** each of the variables for full marks.*

Table 1.1 summarises some information about four stars in the constellation Cygnus.

**Table 1.1**

| **Name** | **Colour** | **Luminosity / L**<sub>**Sun**</sub> |
|---|---|---|
| Aljanah | orange | 62 |
| Deneb | blue-white | 196 000 |
| Fawaris | blue | 155 |

(i) the highest surface temperature,

[1]

[1]

[1]
parts.solution_md:
The star with the...

(i) highest surface temperature is:

- Fawaris; **[1 mark]**

(ii) lowest surface temperature is:

- Aljanah; **[1 mark]**

(iii) largest radius is:

- Deneb; **[1 mark] ** *Accept Sadr*

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *Remember that **blue** is the **hottest** colour possible, while **red** is the **coolest**.*

> *White comes **between **yellow and blue, so yellow-white is hotter than yellow, but blue-white is cooler than blue!*

> *The radius of a star can be estimated using the Stefan-Boltzmann Law*

$L=4πr^{2}σT^{4}\Rightarrowr^{2}\propto\frac{L}{T^{4}}$

> *Since Deneb has the largest luminosity by far, you can expect it to have the largest radius, which it does (≈200 R*<sub>*Sun*</sub>*).*

> *However, due to the power of 4 on **T*<sup>*4*</sup>*, the surface temperature of the star also has a significant impact on a star's radius, so Sadr would also have been an acceptable estimate.*

> *Sadr does not have the largest radius, but it is close to the radius of Deneb since it has a much lower temperature (≈150 R*<sub>*Sun*</sub>*).*

Determine the surface temperature of Sadr:

List the known quantities:

- Surface temperature of Aljanah, $T_{A}$ = 4700 K

Use the graph to determine the peak wavelengths:

![peak-wavelength-wien-graph-ma](assets/008-peak-wavelength-wien-graph-ma.png)

- Aljanah:  $λ_{A}$ = 650 nm **AND **Sadr:  $λ_{S}$ = 400 nm **[1 mark]**

Use Wien's law to determine the surface temperature of Sadr:

- Wien's law:  $T\propto\frac{1}{λ_{max}}$
- Therefore, $\frac{T_{S}}{T_{A}}=\frac{λ_{A}}{λ_{S}}$
- $T_{S}=T_{A}\times\frac{λ_{A}}{λ_{S}}=4700\times\frac{650}{400}$ **[1 mark]**
- $T_{S}$ = 7600 K **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *You must be confident in turning proportionalities into equations.*

> *Since *$T\propto\frac{1}{λ_{max}}$*, this means *$Tλ_{max}=constant$*. This constant is going to be the same for both stars. *

> *Therefore, *$T_{S}λ_{S}=T_{A}λ_{A}\Rightarrow\frac{T_{S}}{T_{A}}=\frac{λ_{A}}{λ_{S}}$*.*

parts.problem_md:
In a comparison of two stars, A and B, the following data was collected

Surface temperature of star A = 25 000 K

Surface temperature of star B = 4300 K

The radius of star B was determined to be 1.1 × 10<sup>5</sup> times larger than the radius of star A.

Calculate the ratio

$\frac{luminosityofstarB}{luminosityofstarA}$
parts.solution_md:
Calculate the ratio of the luminosities of stars A and B:

List the known quantities:

- Surface temperature of star A, $T_{A}$ = 25 000 K
- Surface temperature of star B, $T_{B}$ = 4300 K
- Ratio of radii = $\frac{r_{B}}{r_{A}}=1.1\times10^{5}$

Use the Stefan-Boltzmann law to determine the ratio of the luminosities:

- Stefan-Boltzmann law:  $L=4πr^{2}σT^{4}$
- Ratio:  `L _ B / L _ A = (r _ B ^2 T _ B ^ 4)/(r _ A ^2 T _ A ^ 4) = ( r _ B / r _ A ) ^2 x (T _ B ^ 4 )/(T _ A ^ 4)` **[1 mark]**
- `L _ B / L _ A = (( 1.1 x 10 ^ 5 ) ^2 x ( 4300 ) ^ 4)/(( 25 000 ) ^ 4)` **[1 mark]**
- $\frac{L_{B}}{L_{A}}=1.059\times10^{7}=1.1\times10^{7}$ **[1 mark]**

**[Total: 3 marks]**

> *In the equation *$L=4πr^{2}σT^{4}$*, 4πσ is a **constant**. Therefore, *$\frac{L}{r^{2}T^{4}}=4πσ=constant$*.  *

> *This means *$\frac{L_{B}}{r_{B}^{2}T_{B}^{4}}=\frac{L_{A}}{r_{A}^{2}T_{A}^{4}}$* and *$\frac{L_{B}}{L_{A}}=\frac{r_{B}^{2}T_{B}^{4}}{r_{A}^{2}T_{A}^{4}}$* .*
